title: Research is Brilliant: Research Schools are Average
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Salles argues that research-informed schools do not automatically get better results, pointing to two prominent research schools whose progress scores sit at the median of their comparison groups. His diagnosis is that schools adopt what the research says works without ever measuring whether it raises learning locally. He proposes four questions for implementing research, centred on why X worked, how to do it for maximum impact on learning, how to make it easy for every teacher, and how to measure the result. He backs the stance with his own career habit of measuring impact in grades, including one intervention that lowered his department's progress and was dropped. He applies the same test to popular English ideas such as The Writing Revolution, and closes with three questions: do activities make students work hard, think hard and remember more.
points: Research schools are statistically average on progress, which Salles reads as evidence that enthusiasm for research is not the same as measured impact.
Schools treat research as a recipe (X works, so do X) instead of asking why X worked and how to deliver it for maximum learning.
Consistency of practice across teachers is only a proxy; the goal is learning, so impact has to be measured and the approach tweaked when it is not working.
Salles cites his own failed tutor-time intervention as an example of dropping a practice once its impact was measured and found negative.
His test for any activity is whether it makes students work hard, think hard and remember more.
quotes: They are full of fascinating research and then what seem to me to be very questionable applications of that research. If you’ve followed this newsletter, or read any of my books on teaching, you’ll know I try to test every assumption I have. We are all biased in multiple ways, often without knowing it.
Because we will naturally change our answers to 1-3 if we measure the impact and it is not working. We will always find productive ways to tweak it to make it better.
So from day one as a teacher, I measured my impact. Every grade mattered to me.
Our progress went down, both for maths and English. The whole department did worse because our time and attention was taken away from what makes a difference - the curriculum in the classroom.

It is the change in student self belief that made the difference. Another proof of this is that their data showed this improvement at the pass/fail border. The curriculum did nothing to help students achieve the higher grades.
Research schools don’t measure the impact of their approaches. This is why, most times I read about a strategy, my Spidey senses go into overdrive - danger, danger …very low voltage.
